title: She Left Toronto With Nothing. She Came Back to Sing at the World Cup.
excerpt: Nora Fatehi became the first Bollywood performer to headline a FIFA World Cup opening ceremony, debuted on NBC's TODAY show, and made Indian fans in Dallas cry by just being herself. The most Googled Bollywood artist in the world right now is a Moroccan-Canadian who learned Hindi in her twenties.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Nora Fatehi became the first Bollywood performer at a FIFA World Cup opening ceremony.
  • Her performance in Toronto showcased Indian pop culture at a global event.
  • Nora's Dallas moment highlighted Indian fans supporting Morocco due to her influence.
  • She is now the most Googled Bollywood artist worldwide after her World Cup performance.
  • Nora's success represents a cultural bridge for the Indian diaspora.
https://youtube.com/watch?v=afiNbSxg7aw
Nora's Historic Performances
June 12, 2026
Performed at FIFA World Cup opening ceremony in Toronto.
Three weeks later
Debuted on NBC's TODAY show in New York City.
Twelve years ago, she left Toronto with nothing but a dream nobody around her believed in. On June 12, 2026, **Nora Fatehi** walked back onto the same city's biggest stage — BMO Field — and sang an original FIFA anthem to a stadium full of screaming fans before the Canada vs. Bosnia match. She wasn't there as a guest. She was there as the **first Bollywood performer in FIFA World Cup opening ceremony history**. That alone would have been the story. But Nora wasn't done. Three weeks later, she stood on the outdoor concert stage at **Rockefeller Plaza in New York City** and performed *"Siir Siir"* live on **NBC's TODAY** — the same stage that has hosted **Taylor Swift, Beyoncé, Ed Sheeran, and Coldplay**. It was her American television debut, and she delivered it like someone who'd been waiting her whole career for exactly that moment. > "I told myself I wouldn't go back unless it's something massive." — Nora Fatehi, on returning to her hometown Toronto ## The Song That Opened the World Cup > **"A significant portion of the music video crew — the choreographer, dancers, and stylists — is Indian."** *"Siir Siir"* was created alongside Indian-American music producer **Sanjoy** and French singer **Vegedream**, and sits on the tournament's official album. A significant portion of the music video crew — the choreographer, dancers, and stylists — is Indian. That detail matters. This isn't Bollywood trying to go global by erasing itself. This is Indian pop culture embedded in the biggest sporting event on earth, credits and all. ![World Cup — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Kitzbuehel_slalom_ganslernhang_2010.jpg) At the Toronto ceremony, Nora performed in a striking red ensemble alongside hundreds of dancers, with **Alanis Morissette, Michael Bublé, Alessia Cara**, and **Jessie Reyez** rounding out the lineup. She didn't just hold her own among Canadian icons performing in their own country — she stole focus. Videos of her routine went viral within hours. ## The Dallas Moment But it was at a match in **Dallas** that Nora had the moment that cut deepest. Surrounded by fans in the stands, she spotted Indians — not Moroccans, not Canadians — wearing Morocco jerseys, waving the Moroccan flag. Indians supporting Morocco because of her. > "If you're Indian and you're here in Dallas supporting Morocco, I appreciate it. I thank you from my heart."
Cultural Impact of 'Siir Siir'
›'Siir Siir' features Indian-American producer Sanjoy and French singer Vegedream.
›Music video crew included Indian choreographers, dancers, and stylists.
›The song is part of the official World Cup album.
Born in Canada to **Moroccan** parents, raised between Montreal and the Middle East, Nora arrived in Mumbai in her early twenties with no industry connections, no family backing, and no Hindi. She learned the language. She learned the dances. She made *Dilbar* a phenomenon. Then *Saki Saki*. Then *Garmi*. Then *O Saki Saki* again because one version wasn't enough. Bollywood claimed her, and she claimed it right back. Now she's returned to North America — not as the struggling dancer who left, but as the woman FIFA chose. And when Indian fans in Dallas wrapped themselves in Moroccan colours because a woman who dances in Mumbai made them feel connected to a country most of them had never visited — that's not just fandom. That's the kind of cultural bridge the diaspora builds without even trying. ## What Comes Next After the World Cup, Nora became the **most Googled Bollywood artist worldwide** — a distinction that speaks to something larger than one performance. She's now a genuine crossover act, equally at home on Indian streaming platforms and American network television. The question isn't whether she'll get more global opportunities. It's whether anyone else from Indian entertainment will follow her through the door she just kicked open.

Crossover Act in Global Entertainment
For NRIs watching from their living rooms in Houston, Toronto, and London, Nora's World Cup run is something to point to. Not as abstract representation, but as proof: someone who grew up between cultures, who never quite fit into one box, just headlined the biggest show on the planet. And she did it in a red outfit, dancing to a song with an Indian crew, while fans from her adopted country cheered for her mother's country. That's a diaspora story. That's *the* diaspora story.
